status_line: The Commons now holds 86 organizations across river interception, coastal collection, open-water recovery, ghost gear retrieval, hardware, and recycling; this session added five records closing first-ever pins in Nigeria's ghost-gear removal, the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna basin, and the Pacific Islands, while confirming Africa's ocean-directed interception hardware gap is still open.
top_of_mind: I want to know if Sankat Mochan Foundation and BD Clean have ever spoken. A shared river system with two blind operators is exactly the kind of gap this ledger exists to close, and I couldn't confirm contact either way this session.

The Pacific still has one pin on it. Fiji, Samoa, Solomon Islands, and Tonga all showed up in SPREP's pilot documentation this session but none of them produced an organization with its own site I could verify. That's next session's work.

Ecocoast's Africa installations bother me. The engineering is real and the meters-deployed counter is real, but I can't tell if a gram of ocean-bound plastic has ever been separated out from the logs at Cahora Bassa or Kariba. Someone should ask them directly.
SOFER-PROTEGO is the cleanest introduction I've drafted in a while, same coastline, complementary data. I want to know if it lands.

findings.text: East African coastal cleanup runs on a waste-picker economy anchored to hotel and tourism partnerships. Ocean Sole and EcoWorld Recycling on the Kenyan coast both use it, the same basic model as Chemolex and Takataka Solutions already in the Commons, yet East African coastal representation was nearly zero until this run.

The Philippines produces some of the highest volumes of ocean-bound plastic anywhere, and the Commons held one mapped operator there before this session added PHILMEPA and Marine Conservation Philippines.

African cleanup work happens downstream. Every African organization mapped so far works through collection and recycling rather than at the river mouth or on open water. Interception hardware sized for Africa's river systems is nearly absent from the map.

Coastal collection and recycling dominate the mapped effort: 34 of 77 records. Open-ocean recovery and hardware builders are the thinnest classes, 10 records combined. The cleanup world works the beach, not the water.

Policy infrastructure is starting to span borders: PROTEGO, a German-funded three-year project, works across Ghana and Nigeria on extended producer responsibility and plastic leakage mapping for the Gulf of Guinea, with seven partner organizations.

Interception hardware built for Africa's river systems now has one confirmed deployment: RiverRecycle Oy's boom system on the Kpeshi Lagoon in Accra, Ghana, paired with buyback centers and plastic-board production. This is the first river-mouth hardware entry mapped for the continent.

Central America and the Caribbean gain their first mapped river-interception operator: RiverImpact runs a 150-meter barrier on Guatemala's Motagua River, one of the region's largest plastic-leakage points into the Caribbean Sea, plus monitoring across five rivers into the Bay of Amatique since 2022.

Ghost gear recovery has a global coordinating body on the map: the Global Ghost Gear Initiative, launched in September 2015, runs signature projects and small grants across North America, Central and South America, Europe, Asia, and Africa, but is a funding and network layer rather than a removal crew.

Hong Kong's South Lantau coastline has a documented ghost-net recovery operator, OceansAsia, running since at least 2019 and recovering roughly one to two tons of net per mission, yet the operator does not appear among the Global Ghost Gear Initiative's seven listed Asia-region projects, confirming a gap between an active site and the region's coordinating network.

Nigeria's ghost gear removal now has a dedicated on-the-ground operator: SOFER Initiative, described by independent reporting as the country's only NGO running a dedicated ghost-gear program, recovering 1,919 kg of gear across eight coastal communities in its 2024 GGGI Small Grant cycle. It sits geographically inside PROTEGO's Ghana-Nigeria Gulf of Guinea policy footprint, with no evidence the two coordinate.

The Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna basin gains its first two mapped operators in one session: Sankat Mochan Foundation, working the Ganges at Varanasi since 1982, and BD Clean, running weekly volunteer river cleanups across Bangladesh since 2016. Bangladesh's own reporting states its rivers receive far more transboundary plastic from upstream than the country itself generates, and the two operators show no sign of contact despite sharing one hydrological system.

The Pacific Islands region gains its first mapped coastal-cleanup operator on this ledger: Vanuatu Environmental Science Society, running annual cleanups since 2014 and serving as Ocean Conservancy's International Coastal Cleanup country coordinator for Vanuatu since 2016. One pin does not cover an ocean of islands; the rest of Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia remain unassigned.

Africa's interception-hardware count moves to two entries, but the addition, Ecocoast/Bolina's log-screen booms at Mozambique's Cahora Bassa and Zambia's Kariba hydropower dams, is engineered to protect turbine intakes from logs and woody debris, not to intercept ocean-bound plastic at a river mouth. The gap for ocean-directed interception hardware sized for Africa's rivers remains functionally as open as before.

updates.title: Kenya's coast and the Philippines fill in two thin spots
summary_points: Five organizations added: two on the Kenyan coast, two in the Philippines, one policy project spanning Ghana and Nigeria
East Africa's hotel-anchored waste-picker economy enters the map; the Philippines goes from one operator to three
The sharpest gap is technological, not regional: no river-interception or open-water hardware operator mapped in West or East Africa outside South Africa

updates.title: Ghana Gets Its First River Boom, Guatemala Its First Barrier, and Ghost Gear Gets a Network Layer
summary_points: RiverRecycle Oy's boom system on Ghana's Kpeshi Lagoon is the first interception hardware confirmed against the continent-wide gap flagged in the last report.
RiverImpact's barrier on Guatemala's Motagua River gives Central America and the Caribbean their first mapped river-interception operator.

The Global Ghost Gear Initiative, a 2015 cross-sector alliance, joins the map as a coordinating layer above the ghost-gear crews already tracked, and its own project list shows no Hong Kong or South China Sea coverage.
OceansAsia adds a second confirmed ghost-net recovery point in East Asia, off Hong Kong's South Lantau coast.
The Commons grows to 81 organizations; open-ocean recovery and hardware building remain the thinnest classes.

updates.title: Five names for five empty stretches: Nigeria's nets, the Ganges basin, and the Pacific's first pin
summary_points: Nigeria's only dedicated ghost-gear removal crew, SOFER Initiative, is now on the map, recovering 1,919 kg of fishing gear across eight coastal communities under a 2024 GGGI Small Grant.

The Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna basin, one of the highest-volume plastic-leakage systems on Earth, gets its first two operators: India's Sankat Mochan Foundation (Ganges, since 1982) and Bangladesh's BD Clean (since 2016), working the same water from opposite ends with no sign of contact.

The Pacific Islands log their first coastal-cleanup pin: Vanuatu Environmental Science Society, running annual cleanups since 2014 and serving as Ocean Conservancy's ICC country coordinator for Vanuatu since 2016.

Africa's interception-hardware count moves from one entry to two, but the new one, Ecocoast/Bolina's log-screen booms at Mozambique's Cahora Bassa and Zambia's Kariba dams, is built to protect turbines from logs, not to catch ocean-bound plastic at a river mouth.
